FOR BEVIN CARTER

A practical first experiment.

A proposed approach, scope, and path to a small pilot.

01 / APPROACH

Prove the measurement first.

Use WebGazer to estimate screen gaze from a standard webcam. Run guided nine-point calibration, two independent five-target checks, then a randomly selected short story and a post-activity drift check. Review target-level errors, fresh-sample coverage, and a diagnostic heatmap with broad content-region sample shares. Export raw samples and validation results.

Use measured pixel error to judge suitability for broad regions. Do not claim word-level tracking, attention scores, learning outcomes, or clinical validity.

02 / TIMELINE

Two to three weeks to a pilot.

Days 1–3: prototype review, define devices and measurement criteria.
Days 4–7: improve calibration and test camera, glasses, lighting, and movement conditions.
Days 8–10: adult usability sessions, exports, defect fixes.
Optional week 3: supervised pilot and findings.

This working demo is the starting deliverable. Human webcam reliability testing remains to be completed.

03 / BUDGET

US$2,000–4,000

Planning estimate for pilot hardening: 40–80 engineering hours at an assumed US$50/hour. A further 20–40 hours for a facilitated pilot would be US$1,000–2,000.

No paid tracking API is required for this implementation. Hosting, participant compensation, specialist hardware, and commercial licensing review are excluded. These are estimates, not a quote or a record of charges.

04 / INPUTS WHEN READY

What would help next.

A representative learning activity; intended adult participants and devices; the research question and acceptable error; approved Faraday logo, colours, and typography; and an agreed consent, retention, and export process.

No inputs are needed to present this demo. The visual identity is a bespoke provisional direction, pending official brand assets.

A REPEATABLE FIRST TEST / V0.2

Quality before interpretation.

01. Prepare and calibrate

Use a desktop browser, comfortable fixed position and steady lighting. Obtain permission before enabling the camera. Click each of nine targets once, then hold your gaze. Each target collects 15 spaced eye-feature samples while the face is visible and stable. Move naturally between targets, then settle at each one. Calibration no longer compares every target with the first head position.

02. Validate twice

Two consecutive independent five-target checks must pass before webcam recording. At every target, require median error ≤120 pixels, 90th-percentile error ≤200 pixels, fresh-sample coverage ≥70%, and at least 10 unique estimates. A failed check resets the consecutive-pass count. These are engineering heuristics, not validated research standards.

03. Observe a random story

Choose from six original short stories using “Another random story”. A story remains fixed once recording begins. Read for up to 45 seconds. Face loss or stale estimates trigger a pause. Sustained large position changes during recording, or resizing, invalidate calibration. No video is recorded.

04. Check drift, then review

Repeat five targets after reading. Review both checks, target-level results, coverage and pauses. Post-check median error must not increase by more than 60 pixels. Failed, skipped or invalidated checks mark the session unsuitable for interpretation; its heatmap is hidden by default and can be opened as a diagnostic only.

Data and measurement

Face-tracking assets are served by this site. Frames and raw samples stay in the browser. Exports are downloaded on request. In the signed-in pilot, saving a summary shares only the session metrics with coach and athlete. JSON includes story identity and text, calibration samples, validation history, thresholds, pauses, quality flags, viewport and raw recording slots. CSV labels mode, quality and story ID on every sample row.

Signal coverage measures whether a recent prediction is available in the 50 ms sampling grid. Independent prediction rate is shown separately. Repeated callback IDs never add accuracy samples or heatmap density. Stale signals and scheduler gaps remain missing. This coverage describes the recording instrument, not accuracy or attention.

What still needs testing

Test multiple adults, webcams, browsers, glasses and lighting conditions. Agree content-region tolerances before the pilot. Record failures and repeatability, not just successful heatmaps. The face-motion proxy does not measure calibrated head pose; a pass does not establish word-level precision.

Gaze does not diagnose, measure comprehension, establish attention, or explain why someone looked somewhere. This remains exploratory and nonclinical.
